mcqs.question: Why does the loop insist on a hypothesis a single test can kill outright, rather than a general suspicion?
options: Because vague suspicions take longer to type into a bug tracker
Because a hypothesis vague enough to survive any result teaches you nothing when it's "confirmed"
Because the scientific method requires exactly one hypothesis per session
Because test frameworks reject assertions written as suspicions
mcqs.explanation: A sharp, falsifiable hypothesis makes every test result informative — it either kills the hypothesis or narrows it. A vague suspicion like "something's off with concurrency" can be rationalized as confirmed by almost any outcome, so the cycle burns time without learning anything.

mcqs.question: A bug report describes an intermittent crash with no reliable repro. What should you do before attempting a fix?
options: Apply the most likely-looking fix and monitor production for recurrence
Add broad exception handling around the suspected area to prevent the crash from surfacing
Treat the absence of a reliable repro as the first thing to investigate — what varies between failing and working runs
Wait for a second occurrence before doing any investigation
mcqs.explanation: Without a repro you can't verify any fix — the symptom vanishing could mean you fixed it, hid it, or got lucky with timing. The right first move is to hunt for what differs between runs that fail and runs that don't, since that difference is usually the missing piece of the hypothesis.

mcqs.question: A regression exists somewhere in the last 800 commits. What's the fastest disciplined way to find the introducing commit?
options: Binary search — check the midpoint commit, then repeat on whichever half still fails
Check every commit in chronological order starting from the oldest
Check every commit in reverse chronological order starting from the newest
Read the diffs of all 800 commits to spot a suspicious-looking change
mcqs.explanation: Binary search over the commit range eliminates roughly half the candidates per check, so 800 commits take about 10 checks instead of up to 800. Reading every diff or scanning linearly in either direction scales with the range size instead of its logarithm.

mcqs.question: Which of these is a properly falsifiable debugging hypothesis?
options: "I think it's a threading issue somewhere in the request handler"
"The code looks wrong around the cache layer"
"Something about concurrency is causing this"
"Two threads increment the counter without a lock, so logging its value around each increment under load should show lost updates"
mcqs.explanation: The last option names a specific mechanism and a concrete, checkable prediction — a single logging experiment can confirm or kill it. The other three name a suspect area without a mechanism or a prediction, so almost any result could be rationalized as supporting them.

mcqs.question: You change a null check, a retry, and a lock in the same commit, rerun, and the bug disappears. What's the problem with this approach?
options: Retries should never be added to fix a bug
You now can't attribute the fix to a specific change, so you don't actually know what the bug was
Null checks and locks are incompatible in the same function
The bug is guaranteed to still exist because multiple changes were made
mcqs.explanation: This is shotgun debugging: when several changes land at once, a disappearing symptom doesn't tell you which change mattered, or whether you got lucky with timing. Changing one variable at a time keeps every test result attributable to a specific cause.

mcqs.question: A fix wraps a failing call in a try/catch that silently ignores the exception, and the crash reports stop. Is the bug fixed?
options: Yes, because the observable symptom — the crash — no longer occurs
Not necessarily — the fix has no causal story for why the call failed, which is the sign of a patched symptom rather than a root cause
Yes, as long as the try/catch also logs a warning message
No, because try/catch blocks are never appropriate fixes
mcqs.explanation: A root-cause fix comes with a one-sentence mechanism explaining why the failure happened. Swallowing an exception without that explanation is a classic symptom patch — the underlying defect likely still fires, just silently, and may surface worse later.
